title: SpeedPath pilot - weekly latency review
header: Date: 2026-12-09 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Recording: Yes | Location: Zoom
summary: Weekly POC sync to review time-to-first-token (TTFT) improvements, streaming behavior, sequence length profiles and kernel selection tradeoffs. We validated microburst scenarios on 2 instance types, discussed quantization regressions and next steps for a 48-hour benchmarks run. Action items assigned for a canary rerun, security doc share, and a short demo of streaming reassembly logic.
next_steps: Redwood to run 48h microburst run on g5x2 and a100-equivalent w/ new kernel knobs (Marcus) - due 2026-12-11
Customer to provide 3 representative prompt sets (short/med/long) - Tomás - due 2026-12-10
Lina to share security SOC2 doc subset and private deployment checklist - due 2026-12-12
Schedule 30m demo for streaming reassembly (focus on live aggregation) - Lina to propose times
action_items: Marcus - kick off 48h microburst bench with TTFT profiling flags - 2026-12-09/ongoing
Tomás - upload prompt sets + p95 latency targets to shared sheet - due 2026-12-10
Hannah - provide the list of allowed IP ranges for VPC peering - due 2026-12-13
transcript:
[15:00] Lina Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, we've got 45 minutes, we'll focus on TTFT and the kernel tradeoffs we flipped over last week
[15:01] Priya Nair: cool, thanks Lina. quick status — we ran the internal smoke tests yesterday, saw some improvement but still seeing spikes in the microburst case
[15:02] Marcus Bell: right, the microburst pattern seemed to trigger a fallback path in the runtime, which increased latency to 220ms on short prompts, whereas baseline was ~140ms, so that's what we instrumented
[15:03] Tomás Ruiz: also fwiw our typical prompt distribution is 70% short (<64 tokens), 25% medium (64-256), 5% long, so TTFT matters a lot for us
[15:04] Hannah Lee: yeah and we're sensitive to those spikes, SLOs at p95 200ms for the short path. anything above that flags incidenting which we wanted to avoid
[15:05] Lina Park: okay good context. Marcus can you summarize the knob changes you tried this week?
[15:06] Marcus Bell: sure — main changes were: enable continuous batching threshold down to 8ms, reduce padding-to-batch ratio, and switch from fused-attention kernel to tiled-runner kernels for short sequences in one variant. we also disabled full KV prefetch for the first token path to reduce startup I/O
[15:07] Priya Nair: the tiled-runner — isn't that what caused regression for some of our mid-length cases last month?
[15:07] Marcus Bell: yes there's a tension — tiled is optimized for tiny seq lengths with lower kernel launch overhead but it can be less efficient at 128-256 ranges vs the fused path. we tuned a heuristic to pick tiled when seq_len <= 48 for this pilot
[15:08] Tomás Ruiz: curious, what about quantization — we saw a slight BLEU-ish quality drop in the 4-bit run earlier, was that from a kernel change or quant noise?
[15:09] Marcus Bell: initial analysis says it's quantization + specific kernel math. the fused-attention currently uses a different accumulator precision which helped a little. we're going to pin the quant profiles and rerun with both kernels to isolate the delta
[15:10] Lina Park: makes sense. Hannah, from infra side any constraints for the 48h bench? network? ephemeral disks?
[15:11] Hannah Lee: only that we need to maintain peered VPC for the test cluster, and the firewall-ing must be stable for the entire window. also we want logs forwarded to our SIEM — can you add that to the run?
[15:12] Marcus Bell: yes we can stream logs to your SIEM endpoint, although that adds some telemetry overhead. we'll toggle sampling to avoid adding noise to TTFT numbers
[15:13] Priya Nair: can you clarify what you mean by sampling? we don't want telemetry to be the thing that changes the TTFT profile
[15:14] Marcus Bell: sure — sampling = only 1% of tokens get full trace, others get lightweight metrics. that way the tracer doesn't add tail latency in every request
[15:15] Tomás Ruiz: about streaming — one of our core flows is streaming outputs to web clients where early tokens must show up before finalization, we've had issues with reassembly in the middle of chunked responses
[15:16] Marcus Bell: we added a streaming reassembly layer on the client-side that buffers fragments and applies sequence ordering; the server now emits chunk IDs and offsets. sometimes the transcript had 'first token past' in logs — sorry bad ASR — i mean first token fast path
[15:17] Lina Park: ha the transcription thing again. ok good. did you notice any TTFT difference when streaming was enabled vs non-streaming?
[15:18] Marcus Bell: yes small increase ~10-15ms due to framing headers, but in our clipped-paths we can avoid the overhead by using smaller headers and fewer round trips — we can do a proto change to fold headers into the first packet for short responses
[15:19] Priya Nair: that would help. also, on sequence lengths — is there an option to dynamically pick kernel based on running average sequence length per session?
[15:20] Marcus Bell: we already have a session-level heuristic in the router — it can pick a model variant based on histogram over last N requests. downside: warm start for the chosen kernel's caches might cost you a few ms if it triggers a kernel swap on the GPU
[15:21] Tomás Ruiz: hmm, the swap cost is the pain point. do we have metrics on how long the tiled vs fused kernel take to warm up under our workload?
[15:22] Marcus Bell: preliminary: tiled warms nearly instantly for <=32 tokens, fused better when >96. warm-up delta is ~5-12ms depending on the micro-batching state. but with KV cache priming the first token of a new session is often the outlier
[15:23] Hannah Lee: what's Redwood's recommendation for VPC/private case — pinned kernels per instance or dynamic routing? from an operational POV, pinned reduces unpredictability
[15:24] Lina Park: yes pinned kernels per pool is simpler operationally. dynamic routing buys you percentiles but increases variability; for an enterprise SLO it's common to pin for the critical short-path pool and have a fallback pool for long-form workloads
[15:25] Priya Nair: ok that aligns with what we were thinking. Marcus you mentioned disabling KV prefetch for first-token path — any correctness risk there?
[15:26] Marcus Bell: minimal, it's a trade: prefetch reduces later token latencies but costs initial IO before first token emit. for short responses it's usually better to cut prefetch and live with slightly higher mid-token latencies if needed
[15:27] Tomás Ruiz: can we do partial prefetch? like prime attention layers only for first few layers?
[15:28] Marcus Bell: yeah partial prefetch of top-k layers is possible — reduced IO footprint and still catches hotspot attention windows; that's on the experiment list for the 48h run
[15:29] Priya Nair: any surprise regressions from the recent runtime bump? our earlier week run saw an odd p99 blip at 10am UTC
[15:30] Marcus Bell: that was telemetry noise from a vendor side upgrade, we traced it to a kernel probe that mis-handled a rare padding pattern. patched in the branch we pushed Friday
[15:31] Hannah Lee: good. on encryption: for Private we'll need KMS integration and HSM signing for audit headers — is that in scope for this POC or later?
[15:32] Lina Park: we can include a minimal KMS flow in the Private pilot. full HSM/attestation is usually part of later phase but we can surface the design and checklist now. I'll share the SOC2/security subset doc after this call
[15:33] Tomás Ruiz: one more question on metrics alignment — ttf definitions differ; do you use time-to-first-byte or first-token? our frontend measures TTFB which includes network time to browser
[15:34] Marcus Bell: good point — we report both: server TTFT (time from receive to first token emit at server) and observed TTFB (end-to-end). we'll annotate the benchmark sheet with both fields and include network hop timings
[15:35] Priya Nair: can you send over a sample results CSV format so our SRE can ingest easily?
[15:36] Marcus Bell: yes, will drop a template into the shared drive. includes: timestamp, model_variant, seq_len, server_ttft_ms, client_ttbf_ms, kernel, quant_profile, sample_id
[15:37] Lina Park: quick recap before we run out — Marcus will start the 48h microburst with the two kernel variants and quant pinned, will stream sampled traces to customer's SIEM, and will flag any p95 breach. Tomás will upload prompt sets and SLO targets. Hannah will provide VPC CIDR ranges. I'll share security docs and proposed times for the streaming reassembly demo
[15:38] Tomás Ruiz: sounds good. can we also include one end-to-end run that simulates browser clients with high concurrency?
[15:39] Marcus Bell: yes we can run a WebSocket shaper to emulate 400 concurrent low-latency clients, add that to the bench plan
[15:40] Priya Nair: thanks all, appreciate the thoroughness. any blockers from Redwood for starting the runs now?
[15:41] Marcus Bell: only waiting on the prompt sets and the SIEM endpoint credentials; otherwise we'll kick-off by EOD
[15:42] Hannah Lee: we'll get the SIEM creds to Marcus via the secure share. also note: maintenance window on Monday 06:00-07:00 UTC, avoid scheduling critical runs then
[15:43] Lina Park: noted, thanks Hannah. ok final wrap — Marcus will post initial 6h checkpoint mid-run, full 48h artifacts when done, Lina will follow up with security bundle. any final questions?
[15:44] Priya Nair: none from me. thanks everyone
[15:44] Lina Park: thanks team, see you next week
